question: to the Commission Sophie Wilmès (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Wouter Beke (PPE), Elisabetta Gualmini (Renew), Maria Grapini (S&D), Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew), Michael McNamara (Renew), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Jan-Christoph Oetjen (Renew) Subject:

The revision of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive1 (EPBD) forms part of the EU’s objective to achieve a zero-emission European building stock. While this objective is consistent with the EU’s climate commitments, the ability to achieve it raises important questions, particularly given the diverse building stocks across the Member States. There is a risk of a disconnect between this objective and the efforts required to fulfil it, which could undermine stakeholder support and, ultimately, the achievement of this objective. In the light of this: 1.

Does the Commission intend to establish stronger monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to assess the real feasibility and implementation of national renovation pathways under the EPBD, and based on the use of such strengthened mechanisms, would the Commission envisage a targeted review of the EPBD or would it in any case keep the Directive as it stands to maintain alignment with climate objectives?

Does the Commission envisage introducing greater operational flexibility or countryspecific adaptation mechanisms to reflect the structural disparities between national building stocks and investment capacities?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the investment trajectory required under the EPBD remains financially sustainable and socially acceptable, particularly as regards the capacity of Member States to support vulnerable households affected by energy poverty?
OJ L, 2024/1275, 8.5.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1275/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) Under the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)1, Member States are obliged to regularly review the implementation of minimum energy performance requirements and to prepare and regularly review national building renovation plans, including renovation trajectories. The EPBD requires the Commission to conduct a review by the end of 2028, including an assessment of whether its application, in combination with other legislative instruments, delivers sufficient progress towards a fully decarbonised building stock by 2050. The EPBD already provides ample flexibilities, allowing Member States to tailor measures to their specific national context, including allowing for exemptions that can be justified on unfavourable cost-benefit assessment grounds. The EPBD requires Member States to provide appropriate financial measures and technical assistance, in particular for vulnerable households. The Commission’s March 2026 Report on Energy Efficiency Financing2 promotes the increased use of financial instruments and blended financing solutions, and the recommendation on unlocking private investments3 proposes innovative financing schemes. The Social Climate Fund4 supports vulnerable households, including those in energy poverty. Member States must also use national auction revenues for climate or energy measures, including building decarbonisation while prioritising social aspects.

performance-statements/social-climate-fund_en. The Social Climate Fund will mainly be financed through the emissions trading system for buildings, road transport and additional sectors. Most auction revenues from this system will go to the Member States as national auction revenues.
